title: Subagents
description: Delegate research and parallel work to specialists with their own context.

lessons.title: Meet the Subagents
lessons.description: What they are and when to delegate

theory.title: Specialists with their own shell
theory.body:
A **subagent** is a specialized assistant Claude can hand work to. Each runs in its **own separate context window** with its own system prompt and, optionally, a restricted set of tools.

The subagent does the digging and returns a **summary**, so your main conversation stays clean. Built-ins include:
• **Explore**: fast, read-only codebase search
• **Plan**: gathers context during plan mode
• **general-purpose**: multi-step tasks that explore and act
You can also define your own custom agents (next lesson).

theory.title: When to delegate
theory.body:
Delegate when work is **noisy or parallel**: searching across many files, investigating independent questions at once, or running something with lots of output. Skip it for tiny local edits, where a separate context only adds overhead.

The flow: you ask → Claude picks a subagent by its description → it works in its own context → it returns a summary → your conversation continues with just that summary.

Subagent files live in `.claude/agents/` (project) and `~/.claude/agents/` (personal). The slash command for managing them is `/agents`: in recent versions it reminds you to ask Claude or edit `.claude/agents/`; older versions open an interactive manager.

theory.title: Asking for subagents
theory.body: Claude delegates on its own, but you can be explicit. Name the subagent (or say "in parallel"), give each one a clear, independent job and scope, and say what you want back.
theory.code:
Use the Explore subagent to find every call to
legacyFetch in @src/ and list file:line hits.

Use two subagents in parallel: one maps token issuing in
@src/auth, the other lists permission checks in @src/api.
Combine both into a short summary. Do not edit anything.

exercises.prompt: What is the key benefit of a subagent?
options: It edits files without any permission rules
It works in its own separate context window and returns a summary
It has no tool access at all
It always uses a bigger model
exercises.explanation: A separate context window keeps the subagent's noisy exploration out of your main conversation, which only receives the summary.

exercises.prompt: Which built-in subagent is a fast, read-only codebase searcher?
exercises.explanation: Explore is built for searching and reading code without changing it, which makes it fast and safe to delegate to.

exercises.prompt: Match each subagent to its specialty.
exercises.explanation: Built-ins cover common jobs out of the box, while custom agents encode your own team-specific workflows.

exercises.prompt: You need to understand an unfamiliar auth system quickly. Which prompt is better?
options: Use subagents to investigate in parallel: one maps how tokens are issued in src/auth, another finds every permission check in src/api. Report file paths and a short summary of each.
exercises.explanation: Independent questions can run side by side in separate contexts, so splitting them is faster and keeps each answer focused.

exercises.prompt: Which task is the WORST fit for a subagent?
options: Searching 200 files for every use of a deprecated API
Investigating three unrelated bugs in parallel
Running a test suite with thousands of lines of output
Fixing a one-character typo in the file you are already editing
exercises.explanation: A separate context only pays off for big or noisy work, so a tiny local edit just gains overhead.

exercises.prompt: Put the delegation flow in order.
steps: You ask for a broad investigation
Claude picks a subagent based on its description
The subagent works in its own context window
The main conversation continues with just the summary
exercises.explanation: Only the summary comes back, which is exactly why delegation keeps your main context small.

exercises.prompt: Inside a session, type the slash command for managing subagents.
exercises.explanation: `/agents` is the entry point for subagents: recent versions point you to asking Claude or editing `.claude/agents/`, older ones open a manager.

exercises.scenario: Before upgrading from React 18 to 19, you want two things investigated at the same time: usage of deprecated APIs and how well the components are covered by tests.
exercises.sample: We're upgrading from React 18 to 19 (see @package.json). Use two subagents in parallel. One: search @src/components/ for APIs deprecated or removed in React 19 (e.g. string refs, legacy context, defaultProps on function components) and list file:line hits. Two: report which components in @src/components/ have no tests. Constraint: do not edit anything. Done when you combine both into a short upgrade-risk report ranked by risk.
exercises.explanation: Giving context, independent tasks, scope and the combined deliverable lets the subagents work in parallel without overlap.

theory.title: Anatomy of an agent file
theory.body:
A custom subagent is a Markdown file: `.claude/agents/<name>.md` (project, commit it to share) or `~/.claude/agents/<name>.md` (personal). Like commands and skills, it starts with **YAML frontmatter** between `---` lines (`key: value` per line), and the **body below is the agent's system prompt**.
• `name:` unique identifier (required)
• `description:` when Claude should delegate to it (required)
• `tools:` comma-separated list of allowed tools (optional; **omit it and the agent inherits every tool** available to subagents)
• `model:` `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku` or `inherit` (optional)
theory.code:
---
name: code-reviewer
description: Reviews code for quality and best practices.
  Use after code changes.
tools: Read, Glob, Grep
model: sonnet
---

You are a code reviewer. When invoked, analyze the code and
provide specific, actionable feedback on quality, security,
and best practices.

theory.title: Restrict and describe
theory.body:
Give an agent only the tools it needs: a reviewer that only reads gets `tools: Read, Glob, Grep`, so it can't edit anything.

Write the `description` as a trigger: say **what it does and when to use it** ("Runs the test suite and fixes failures. Use proactively after code changes."). Vague descriptions like "helps with tests" rarely get picked.

If a project agent and a personal agent share a name, the project one wins.

theory.title: Calling your specialist
theory.body:
Three ways to use it:
• Let Claude delegate automatically when the description matches.
• Ask explicitly: "Use the test-runner subagent to fix failing tests".
• Run a **whole session** as the agent with the `--agent` flag (singular) followed by its name.

exercises.prompt: Which frontmatter fields are required in a subagent file?
exercises.explanation: Claude needs a name to identify the agent and a description to know when to use it; everything else has a sensible default.

exercises.prompt: What happens if you omit `tools` from an agent file?
options: It inherits every tool available to subagents
It gets no tools at all
exercises.explanation: Omitting `tools` means the agent inherits every tool available, so you list tools only when you want to restrict it.

exercises.prompt: Where does a project subagent you want to share with your team go?
exercises.explanation: Files in `.claude/agents/` are committed with the repo, so every teammate gets the same agent.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of an agent file to its job.
exercises.explanation: Frontmatter configures who the agent is and what it may use, while the body is the system prompt that shapes how it behaves.

exercises.prompt: Which description will get your test agent used at the right times?
options: description: Runs the test suite, diagnoses failures and fixes them. Use proactively after code changes.
exercises.explanation: Claude delegates by matching tasks against the description, so a specific "what and when" gets the agent used at the right times.

exercises.prompt: Complete this read-only reviewer agent that runs on Sonnet.
exercises.code:
---
name: code-reviewer
___: Reviews changed code for bugs and security issues. Use after code changes.
___: Read, Grep, Glob
model: ___
---
You are a senior code reviewer...
exercises.explanation: `description` tells Claude when to delegate, `tools` limits the reviewer to reading, and `model` chooses which model runs it.
exercises.hint: Frontmatter keys: name, description (when to delegate), tools (comma list), model (sonnet, opus, haiku or inherit).

exercises.prompt: Create a test-runner subagent and use it.
steps: Restrict tools to what it needs
Write the system prompt in the body
Say: Use the test-runner subagent to fix failing tests
exercises.explanation: Restricting tools before writing the prompt keeps the agent safe, and naming it explicitly guarantees it gets used.

exercises.prompt: Start a whole new session running as your `code-reviewer` subagent, using the `--agent` flag.
exercises.explanation: `--agent` makes the named agent the main agent for the whole session, so its prompt and tool limits apply from the start.

mission.title: Agent Wrangler
mission.intro: Kip has a crew now. Delegate real work to subagents in one of your repos.
checklist: Ask Claude to use the Explore subagent to map how one feature works in your repo
Create `.claude/agents/code-reviewer.md` with name, description and `tools: Read, Grep, Glob`
Make a small change, then say "Use the code-reviewer subagent to review my changes"
Run `/context` and notice how little of the main context the review used
mission.explanation: Subagents keep heavy research and reviews out of your main context.
